reply_acts.text: (kimi-1 kind map) kimi-1 is now mapping Lean's 1,724 Init syntax kinds to the port's grammar declarations. It reads them from the port's cache, not from a startup run, so it doesn't depend on kimi-5's memory problem. The job is `invoke-1790817794707-29491-f4f06590`, parked as `park-1f9445cf…`.

reply_acts.author: claude-4
reply_acts.text: (what it produces) `/tmp/pyreg/state/kind-map.tsv` will have one row per Lean kind, in one of three classes: builtin, added by Init's own syntax, or antiquotation. Each row records the port declaration that produces the kind, or a blank. The README gives counts per class and per status, with sample missing kinds cited to where Lean declares them. It also checks itself: `declaration` and an Init array notation must show as present, and a planted bogus kind must show as missing. Whether each declared kind compiles is a separate job, for after this one.

previous_reply_acts.text: (two Codex jobs, running) I read "these issues" as the two I'd held back, and both are now running. codex-4 is finding out why a one-line compiler edit costs a 10-minute rebuild. codex-6 is checking the `primitives` module error. Each works in its own worktree, apart from kimi-5's, and I'm parked on both, so their results will be in the morning summary.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (codex-4, speed) `invoke-1790817669815-29488-0c3c50ed`, parked as `park-c86dfcc5…`. This is discovery only, with no code changes. It profiles the 644 s edit case and measures how much of the rebuild regenerates files that come out byte-identical. It also looks at how Lean and Lake decide a module's output can be reused, then proposes the smallest change so an edit rebuilds only what it affects. It writes this to `/tmp/pyreg/overnight/SPEED.md`. If the proposal holds up, the implementation goes out as a separate job.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (codex-6, `primitives`) `invoke-1790817675299-29489-727b0325`, parked as `park-74b014c1…`. It first reruns `namedName`, `macroArg` and `precedence` through the verdict driver, which uses the same demand resolution as startup, at the current branch head. If the error doesn't appear, it came from kimi-3's smaller harness and the job stops there. If it does, codex-6 finds where the module should come from and fixes it only if the fix is small, with a test that fails without the fix.
